What is digital frequency, and where is Nyquist?
column2: ω = 2πf/f_s in rad/sample; the Nyquist frequency f_s/2 is ω = π, and ω is periodic in 2π.

column1: A 9 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz with no filter. Where does it appear?
column2: At 1 kHz: f and f + m·f_s give identical samples, and a real tone folds into [0, f_s/2].

column1: Frequency response of the N-point moving average?
column2: |H| = |sin(Nω/2)/(N sin(ω/2))|: gain 1 at DC, nulls at m·f_s/N, delay (N − 1)/2 samples, noise variance gain 1/N.

column1: EMA y[n] = (1 − α)y[n − 1] + αx[n]: time constant and noise gain?
column2: Time constant ≈ 1/α − 1/2 samples; white-noise variance gain α/(2 − α). One multiply and one state replace a long average.

column1: When is a causal LTI system BIBO stable?
column2: When Σ|h[n]| < ∞, equivalently when every pole of H(z) lies strictly inside the unit circle.

column1: How many extra bits does a sum of N terms need?
column2: ⌈log₂N⌉ guard bits in the worst case (all terms at full scale with the same sign).

column1: At 45 nm, how do an instruction and a 32-bit add compare in energy?
column2: About 70 pJ of processor overhead per instruction against 0.1 pJ for a 32-bit add (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014): control and data movement dominate arithmetic.

column1: How do pole radius and bandwidth relate near the unit circle?
column2: A pole at radius r gives a −3 dB width ≈ 2(1 − r) rad/sample, i.e. Δf ≈ (1 − r)f_s/π.

column1: Time constant of a pole at radius r?
column2: τ = −1/ln r ≈ 1/(1 − r) samples; width × time constant ≈ 2, so a narrow filter rings for a long time.

column1: Write a second-order notch at ω₀.
column2: H(z) = g(1 − 2cos ω₀ z⁻¹ + z⁻²)/(1 − 2r cos ω₀ z⁻¹ + r²z⁻²): zeros on the circle null ω₀, poles at radius r set the width; g = 1/H(1) for unit DC gain.

column1: What is group delay and why budget it rather than phase?
column2: τ_g = −dφ/dω (samples): the delay of a narrowband envelope. A pure delay z^(−D) has τ_g = D at all ω.

column1: Group delay of a pole at its own angle?
column2: About ρ/(1 − ρ) samples: 19 at ρ = 0.95, 99 at 0.99. Sharp IIR filters have large delay near the band edge.

column1: What does a first-order all-pass do?
column2: (z⁻¹ − a)/(1 − az⁻¹) has |H| = 1 everywhere and delays DC by (1 + a)/(1 − a) samples: phase shaping with no magnitude change.

column1: What does reflecting a zero to 1/z* do?
column2: Keeps |H| (up to a constant) and changes the phase; a filter with all zeros inside the circle is minimum phase, with the least delay for its magnitude.

column1: Define the N-point DFT and its relation to the DTFT.
column2: X[k] = Σ x[n]W_N^(kn), W_N = e^(−j2π/N): samples of the DTFT at ω_k = 2πk/N.

column1: DFT bin spacing and the on-bin amplitude rule?
column2: Spacing f_s/N (one over the record length); a tone of amplitude A exactly on bin k₀ gives |X[k₀]| = AN/2 in bins k₀ and N − k₀.

column1: When does circular convolution equal linear convolution?
column2: When N ≥ L + M − 1 for sequences of lengths L and M; otherwise the tail wraps around.

column1: How many valid outputs does overlap-save give per block?
column2: N − M + 1 for an M-tap filter and N-point FFTs: the first M − 1 outputs are corrupted by wrap-around and discarded.

column1: When does FFT (fast) convolution beat direct filtering?
column2: Per output it costs ≈ 4(N log₂N + N)/(N − M + 1) real multiplies against M direct; with the course's model the crossover is near 44 taps.

column1: Symmetry of the DFT of a real signal?
column2: X[N − k] = X[k]*: magnitudes are even, phases odd, so only bins 0 to N/2 carry information.

column1: What does zero-padding a record do?
column2: Samples the same DTFT more finely; it interpolates the spectrum but adds no resolution, which is set by the record length.

column1: How does radix-2 decimation in time split a DFT?
column2: Into DFTs G and H of the even and odd samples: X[k] = G[k] + W_N^k H[k], X[k + N/2] = G[k] − W_N^k H[k] (a butterfly).

column1: Operation count of a radix-2 FFT?
column2: log₂N stages of N/2 butterflies: (N/2)log₂N complex multiplies and N log₂N complex adds; saving 2N/log₂N over the direct N².

column1: How many twiddle multiplications are non-trivial?
column2: (N/2)log₂N − 3N/2 + 2 (3,586 for N = 1024): W⁰ = 1 and W^(N/4) = −j need no multiplier.

column1: Why does hardware like radix-4?
column2: Its 4-point butterfly's internal twiddles are ±1, ±j, so it needs (3N/8)log₂N complex multiplies: 75% of radix-2.

column1: What is an R2SDF FFT pipeline?
column2: One butterfly per stage with delay-line feedback: log₂N butterflies, log₂N − 2 general multipliers, N − 1 delay words, one sample per clock.

column1: Why does a fixed-point FFT scale by 1/2 per stage, and what does it cost?
column2: Each stage can double a magnitude (N overall); scaling keeps word width and yields X/N, but each shift discards a bit (rounding noise, lost small-signal range) and one component can still grow by 1 + √2.

column1: What is block floating point in an FFT?
column2: Scale a stage by 1/2 only when its data actually grow, and keep one shared exponent for the block.

column1: What is spectral leakage?
column2: A tone not on a bin spreads into all bins, because the record's finite length multiplies the signal by a window: its spectrum is convolved with the window's.

column1: Define a window's coherent gain and ENBW.
column2: CG = (1/N)Σw; ENBW = NΣw²/(Σw)² bins: the noise bandwidth each bin collects relative to the tone.

column1: Rectangular vs Hann window figures?
column2: Rectangular: ENBW 1, sidelobes −13.3 dB, scalloping −3.92 dB. Hann: CG 0.5, ENBW 1.5, sidelobes −31.5 dB, scalloping −1.42 dB.

column1: How far below a tone does an FFT's noise floor sit?
column2: SNR + 10log₁₀(N/(2·ENBW)) dB. The 10log₁₀(N/2) term is the FFT's processing gain: longer records lower the floor without changing the SNR.

column1: How do you choose a coherent ADC test frequency?
column2: f_in = k·f_s/N with k relatively prime to N (any odd k when N = 2^m): an integer number of cycles, every code exercised, no window needed.

column1: Define ENOB and its full-scale caveat.
column2: ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02 for a full-scale test; a test at −x dBFS should add x dB to the SINAD (refer it to full scale) or ENOB reads low.

column1: Ideal SNR of a B-bit converter?
column2: 6.02B + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine: 74.0 dB at 12 bits, 98.1 dB at 16.

column1: How noisy is a periodogram bin, and how do you fix it?
column2: Its standard deviation equals its mean; averaging K segments (Welch) reduces it by √K at the cost of resolution.

column1: What do the four linear-phase FIR types force?
column2: Symmetric taps, M even (I): no forced zero. Symmetric, M odd (II): zero at π. Antisymmetric, M even (III): zeros at 0 and π. Antisymmetric, M odd (IV): zero at 0.

column1: Delay of a linear-phase FIR of order M?
column2: M/2 samples at every frequency, M/(2f_s) seconds: sharpness costs latency.

column1: What is the Gibbs phenomenon in FIR design?
column2: Truncating the ideal response gives an overshoot of 8.95% of the jump (first stopband lobe ≈ −21 dB) at any length; only a tapered window lowers it.

column1: Window-method stopband errors?
column2: Rectangular −21 dB, Hann −44 dB, Hamming about −53 dB, Blackman −75 dB, with transition ≈ 2πD/M, D ≈ 0.9, 3.1, 3.3, 5.6.

column1: Kaiser's design formulas?
Why does an equiripple design beat a window design?
column2: It weights the bands (W = δ_p/δ_s) and spreads the error evenly, so it exploits a looser passband tolerance; order ≈ (−10log₁₀(δ_pδ_s) − 13)/(2.324Δω).

column1: What does the alternation theorem say?
column2: The minimax-optimal type I filter's weighted error has at least L + 2 alternating extrema of equal size (L = M/2); Parks–McClellan iterates to it.

column1: How many multipliers does a symmetric FIR need?
column2: ⌈(M + 1)/2⌉ per output with folding: add the two samples that share a coefficient first (the DSP block's pre-adder).

column1: Convert 0.1 dB peak-to-peak ripple and 60 dB to δ's.
What is the discrimination D of a filter specification?
column2: D = (10^(A_s/10) − 1)/(10^(A_p/10) − 1): how much the band edges' power gains must be separated.

column1: Butterworth and Chebyshev I order bounds?
column2: Butterworth N ≥ log₁₀D/(2log₁₀(Ω_s/Ω_p)); Chebyshev N ≥ arccosh√D/arccosh(Ω_s/Ω_p): logarithmic growth, so far lower for sharp edges.

column1: Rank Butterworth, Chebyshev and elliptic filters.
column2: For the same mask: Butterworth (maximally flat) needs the highest order, Chebyshev I (equiripple passband) less, elliptic (equiripple in both bands) the least.

column1: What does the bilinear transform do to frequency?
column2: s = 2f_s(1 − z⁻¹)/(1 + z⁻¹) maps the whole analog axis onto (−π, π) via Ω = 2f_s tan(ω/2): no aliasing, but a warped axis.

column1: Why prewarp the band edges?
column2: So the transform carries the analog edges exactly onto the digital ones; unwarped, a 1 kHz edge at 8 kHz lands at 952.9 Hz.

column1: What is impulse invariance and its flaw?
column2: h[n] = T·h_a(nT), pole s_k → e^(s_kT); the analog response above f_s/2 aliases into the band, so it fails for high-pass and band-stop prototypes.

column1: Why are IIR filters built as cascaded biquads?
column2: High-order direct forms are hypersensitive to coefficient rounding; second-order sections keep each pole pair's sensitivity local. Cost: 5 multiplications per section, 3 when b₀ = b₂ = 1.

column1: When does an IIR filter beat an FIR on multiplications, and when not?
column2: For sharp, narrow transitions (4.9× fewer in 16-07's audio example). For wide transitions relative to f_s the FIR shrinks as 1/Δω and the advantage vanishes.

column1: DF I versus DF II?
column2: Same 2N + 1 multipliers; DF I has 2N delays and only a wide accumulator internally; DF II shares N delays but its internal state x/A can be much larger than the input.

column1: Why do FPGAs use the transposed FIR form?
column2: Its critical path is one multiplier plus one adder at any length; the direct form's adder chain grows with the taps (a tree only to log₂ taps levels).

column1: Why are clustered poles fragile in direct form?
column2: ∂p_i/∂a_k = −p_i^(N−k)/Π_(j≠i)(p_i − p_j): close poles make the denominator tiny, so a small coefficient error moves the poles a lot.

column1: Biquad pole-angle sensitivity?
column2: 1/(2ρ sin θ): large near DC and Nyquist, which is why narrowband low-frequency filters need extra coefficient bits or a coupled form.

column1: How does a lattice show stability?
column2: The step-down recursion k_m = a_m^(m), A_(m−1) = (A_m − k_m z^(−m)A_m(z⁻¹))/(1 − k_m²) gives reflection coefficients; stable iff all |k_m| < 1.

column1: Reflection coefficients of a biquad?
column2: k₂ = a₂ and k₁ = a₁/(1 + a₂); k₂ = ρ² is the product of the pole radii.

column1: How are cascade sections paired, ordered and scaled?
column2: Pair each pole pair with its nearest zeros, place the poles far from the circle first, and scale each section with L∞ or L₂ norms so no internal node overflows.

column1: How wide is a biquad's accumulator for 16-bit data?
column2: Five 16 × 16 products need 35 bits; 40-bit accumulators are common, with rounding and saturation only at the output.

column1: What does downsampling by M do to a spectrum?
column2: Y(e^jω) = (1/M)Σ_k X(e^(j(ω − 2πk)/M)): stretched copies that alias unless X is band-limited to π/M.

column1: What does upsampling by L do?
column2: Inserts L − 1 zeros: X(e^(jωL)) has L − 1 images, removed by an anti-imaging filter with gain L.

column1: State the noble identities.
column2: H(z^M) then ↓M equals ↓M then H(z); ↑L then H(z^L) equals H(z) then ↑L.

column1: What is polyphase decomposition, and what does it save?
column2: H(z) = Σ_p z^(−p)E_p(z^M) with e_p[n] = h[nM + p]; each branch runs at the low rate, saving a factor M (or L).

column1: How is 44.1 kHz converted to 48 kHz?
column2: Rationally by L/M = 160/147: upsample, one filter at the intermediate rate with cutoff min(π/L, π/M), downsample, all implemented polyphase.

column1: Why are half-band filters cheap?
column2: Middle tap 1/2 and every other tap zero: 4K + 3 taps need only K + 1 folded multipliers; ideal for factor-2 stages.

column1: CIC filter response, gain and growth?
column2: H = ((1 − z^(−R))/(1 − z⁻¹))^N: |sin(πfR/f_s)/sin(πf/f_s)|^N, DC gain R^N, register growth N·log₂R bits, no multipliers.

column1: Why may a CIC's integrators overflow?
column2: Two's-complement arithmetic is modulo 2^W, and the combs' differences are exact modulo 2^W as long as the true output fits in W bits.

column1: The additive noise model of rounding?
column2: Error uniform on [−Δ/2, Δ/2], white and uncorrelated with the signal, power Δ²/12; valid for busy signals, not small or periodic ones.

column1: Derive 6.02N + 1.76 dB in one line.
column2: Full-scale sine power 1/2 over Δ²/12 with Δ = 2^(1−N): 1.5·4^N, i.e. 10log₁₀1.5 + 20N log₁₀2.

column1: What is the loading factor, and its optimum?
column2: L = full scale/σ for a Gaussian signal: SQNR = 6.02N + 4.77 − 20log₁₀L before clipping; the optimum is about 5 (12 bits) to 6 (16 bits).

column1: What does Q1.15 mean?
column2: 16-bit two's complement with 1 integer (sign) bit and 15 fraction bits: range [−1, 1 − 2^(−15)], step 3.05 × 10⁻⁵.

column1: What does TPDF dither do, and cost?
column2: ±1 LSB triangular noise added before quantizing makes the error's first two moments independent of the signal (harmonics vanish) at 3× the noise power (+4.8 dB).

column1: What is noise gain?
column2: Σg[n]² from a rounding point to the output: the factor by which that point's Δ²/12 is amplified; 1/(1 − a²) for a first-order pole at a.

column1: What is the dead band of a first-order recursion?
column2: Zero-input y = Q(a·y) sticks at |k| ≤ 1/(2(1 − |a|)) LSB: 5 LSB for a = 0.9, a granular limit cycle.

column1: Why must recursive filters saturate?
column2: Wrap-around turns a large positive value into a large negative one that the feedback can sustain: a full-scale overflow limit cycle from a stable filter.

column1: How wide must a MAC's product and accumulator be?
column2: Product b_x + b_c bits; accumulator adds ⌈log₂N⌉ guard bits for N terms (40 bits for 16 × 16 over 256 taps).

column1: How many multipliers does a filter need?
column2: ⌈(multiplications per output × f_s)/f_clk⌉: folding time-shares fast hardware across taps; unfolding parallelizes for f_s > f_clk.

column1: What is the iteration bound?
column2: T∞ = max over loops of (loop computation time)/(loop registers): no pipelining or retiming can clock a recursion faster.

column1: What does look-ahead do to a recursion?
column2: y[n] = a^M y[n − M] + Σ_(i<M) a^i x[n − i] puts M registers in the loop, dividing the iteration bound by M; the extra feed-forward terms pipeline freely.

column1: What is canonical signed digit (CSD)?
column2: A signed-digit form with no two adjacent non-zero digits; adders = non-zero digits − 1 (0.875 = 1 − 2⁻³ needs one subtractor).

column1: Why do bits cost quadratically in multipliers?
column2: Array multiplier area grows with the product of the widths: at 45 nm an 8-bit multiply is 0.2 pJ against 3.1 pJ at 32 bits (15.5×).

column1: Write the CORDIC iteration.
column2: x_(i+1) = x_i − d_i y_i 2^(−i), y_(i+1) = y_i + d_i x_i 2^(−i), z_(i+1) = z_i − d_i arctan 2^(−i); only shifts and adds.

column1: CORDIC gain, range and convergence?
column2: K = Π√(1 + 2^(−2i)) → 1.64676 (corrected once); range ±99.88°; about one bit of angle per iteration.

column1: Rotation versus vectoring mode?
column2: Rotation (d_i = sign z_i, start z = θ) gives cos θ and sin θ (NCOs, mixers); vectoring (d_i = −sign y_i) gives magnitude and angle.
